grammar.sentence: This is the house ___ I was born.
grammar.ja: これは私が生まれた家です。
grammar.point: 関係副詞 where（場所を説明する）

choices.explain: 先行詞が場所（the house）で、後ろに完全な文が続くので関係副詞 where を使います。
which の後は主語や目的語が欠けた文になりますが、ここは完全な文です。
who は人を先行詞にするときに使います。house は人ではありません。
when は時を表す先行詞に使います。house（場所）には合いません。

grammar.sentence: She said that she ___ tired that day.
grammar.ja: 彼女はその日疲れていると言いました。
grammar.point: 話法（時制の一致）：現在→過去

choices.explain: 主節の動詞（said）が過去なので、that節の中も時制を一致させて was にします。
主節が過去形のとき、that節も過去形に一致させます。
現在完了形はこの文脈の時制の一致には合いません。
be はそのままの形では文の動詞として使えません。

grammar.sentence: If I ___ you, I would accept the offer.
grammar.ja: もし私があなたなら、その申し出を受けるだろう。
grammar.point: 仮定法過去（現在の事実に反する仮定：If + 主語 + were）

choices.explain: 仮定法過去では be動詞は主語に関係なく were を使うのが基本です。
仮定法過去では am ではなく were を使います。

reading.title: A School Garden Project
reading.passage: Last spring, a high school in Nagano started a new project: growing vegetables in an unused corner of the schoolyard. At first, only a few students volunteered, but as the tomatoes and cucumbers began to grow, more classmates became interested and asked to help. Teachers noticed that students who rarely spoke to each other in class started working together, sharing tips about watering and checking for pests. In autumn, the club harvested enough vegetables to donate to a local food bank, and some students used the vegetables in a cooking class. The teacher in charge says the project has taught students not only about farming but also about teamwork and where their food actually comes from.

reading.title: Bees in the City
reading.passage: In several major cities, residents have begun keeping beehives on the rooftops of apartment buildings and offices. Unlike farms in the countryside, cities offer bees a surprising variety of flowers from parks, gardens, and even balconies, which some beekeepers say makes urban honey taste more complex than honey from a single crop. Supporters argue that the hobby also raises awareness about the decline of bee populations, an issue that affects the pollination of many food crops worldwide. However, city officials note that beehives must be placed carefully, since bees can startle people who are unfamiliar with them, and a few neighbors have complained about safety.

reading.title: Saving a Local Dialect
reading.passage: In a small region of Japan, fewer than a thousand elderly residents still speak a traditional local dialect fluently, and linguists warn that it could disappear within a generation. To preserve it, a group of university students has been visiting elderly speakers to record conversations and create a digital dictionary of dialect words and their standard Japanese equivalents. Some younger residents initially found the dialect embarrassing to use in public, associating it with being old-fashioned, but the project has encouraged a few local schools to include dialect lessons in cultural studies classes, hoping to change that perception before the language is lost entirely.

reading.title: Delivery Apps and Local Restaurants
reading.passage: Food delivery apps have become extremely popular in Japanese cities over the past several years, allowing small restaurants to reach customers who would never have visited in person. For many family-run shops, the apps have provided a valuable source of extra income, especially during slow weekday afternoons. However, some restaurant owners complain that the commission fees charged by delivery companies, often around thirty percent of each order, make it difficult to earn a real profit even when order volume is high. A few restaurants have responded by raising delivery-only menu prices slightly, while others have started offering delivery directly through their own websites to avoid the fees entirely.

reading.title: Pen Pals Across Generations
reading.passage: A nursing home and a nearby middle school recently started a pen pal program in which students exchange handwritten letters with elderly residents once a month. Organizers hoped the program would simply bring a little joy to residents who receive few visitors, but the results have gone further than expected. Several students say the letters have changed how they think about aging, since many residents write vivid stories about historical events they experienced firsthand. Meanwhile, staff at the nursing home report that residents who exchange letters seem noticeably more cheerful on the days when new letters arrive, checking the mail with visible excitement.
